ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Savannah, Georgia
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Savannah, Georgia: wall-thickness surveys on corroded piping, vessels, tanks and crane structure, and angle-beam examination of groove welds in carbon steel. The work serves container-terminal equipment, paper and chemical process plants, shipyard and marine steel, and fabrication shops around Chatham County and the Savannah River corridor. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Send your component list through the UT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Savannah

Savannah is a working port city first. Garden City Terminal is the largest single-terminal container facility in the Western Hemisphere by acreage, with dozens of ship-to-shore cranes and well over two hundred rubber-tired gantry cranes moving boxes between ships, stacks, trucks and rail. Behind the terminals sit paper mills, sugar refining on the river, bulk and liquid storage, and a growing aerospace and automotive supply base. Each of these has steel that loses wall to corrosion or carries welds that have to be proven sound.

  • Terminal equipment: crane boom and portal-leg plate, spreader frames, and the structural welds on gantry rails and runway supports, where thickness loss from salt air and cracks from cyclic loading both matter.
  • Paper and pulp mills: steam and condensate piping, digester and recovery-area vessels, dryer-section headers, process water lines and stainless equipment that sees hot, wet, chemically aggressive service.
  • Bulk, liquid and food-process storage: atmospheric tank shells and floors, sugar and syrup tanks, fuel storage near the harbor, and the pipe racks that connect them.
  • Marine and shipyard steel: hull plate and deck structure on vessels visiting for repair, ballast tank boundaries, pilings, dock fittings and fender supports.
  • Aerospace and industrial support: ground-support equipment, hangar structure, jacks and fabricated tooling for the business-jet manufacturing and service cluster around the city's airports.

The common thread is carbon steel in a humid, salt-laden climate. Ultrasonic testing reads the metal that is left, so an owner can decide whether to run, repair or replace.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

A transducer sends a short sound pulse into the steel, and the instrument times the echo from the back wall or from a reflector inside the metal. Because sound velocity in steel is known, time converts to distance. That makes UT the working method for thickness measurement and for volumetric examination of welds, because it sees inside the section rather than only at the surface.

  • It finds: general wall loss, pitting depth under a reading, laminations in plate, internal corrosion on the far side of a pipe, and in welds lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag lines that sit away from the surface.
  • It can miss or misread: shallow surface cracks lying in the dead zone just under the probe, flaws oriented parallel to the beam, discontinuities hidden by rough scale or heavy coating, and anything in coarse-grained cast or austenitic material where sound scatters.
  • It needs: an accessible, reasonably smooth surface, couplant between probe and metal, a calibration block with a known thickness, and a technician who understands what the screen is showing.

Where the question is surface cracking on a ferromagnetic weld, magnetic particle inspection in Savannah is the sharper tool. UT answers the question of what is inside and how thick it is.

How a thickness survey is carried out

A corrosion survey starts with a list of condition monitoring locations, often shortened to CMLs, and a grid or point map for each component. At each point the technician cleans a patch of surface, applies couplant and takes a reading with a dual-element probe. Dual-element probes keep separate transmitting and receiving crystals, which is why they cope with pitted, rough or lightly corroded outside surfaces better than a single-crystal probe.

  1. Calibrate on a step block of the same material and across the range of thickness expected, with the temperature of the block close to the temperature of the part.
  2. Verify on the block again after the work and at any change of probe, cable or instrument.
  3. Read with the A-scan visible. Watching the waveform, not only the digital number, is how a technician spots a double-echo error on thin wall or a reading dropping into a pit.
  4. Record the lowest valid reading and the position, and compare against the previous survey, the nominal wall and the minimum required thickness.

Hot piping is common at the mills. High-temperature probes and couplant exist for that service, and readings are corrected for the temperature of the metal. The method is covered in ASTM E797 and in ASME Section V thickness measurement requirements; the owner's inspection program decides how often each location is read.

Ultrasonic examination of welds

For groove welds, the technician uses an angle-beam shear-wave probe, normally 45, 60 or 70 degrees, so the beam crosses the weld at an angle that suits likely flaw orientation. A reference level, or distance-amplitude curve, is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block so that indication amplitude can be judged against the code. The technician scans the weld from both sides where access allows, moves the probe in a pattern that covers the full volume and the heat-affected zone, and evaluates every indication that crosses the recording level.

This is the work behind structural steel for terminal buildings and crane runways, pressure piping and vessel nozzle welds, and heavy plate repair. Acceptance depends on the governing code, and the code your owner or engineer names decides the method of examination in the first place.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Savannah work

The code on your drawing or in your contract is the rule we apply. For ultrasonic work in this region that usually means one of the following.

  • ASME Section V: Article 4 for ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 for materials, and Article 23 for thickness measurement practice such as SE-797.
  • AWS D1.1: structural welding code for steel, including ultrasonic examination of groove welds and its own acceptance and rejection tables.
  • ASME B31.3 and B31.1: process piping at chemical plants and power piping at mills, with examination types and acceptance in the piping code tables.
  • ASME Section VIII Division 1: Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds in pressure vessels.
  • API 510, 570 and 653: the in-service inspection codes for vessels, piping and aboveground tanks. Your authorized inspector holds responsibility for the inspection; Atlantis supplies the thickness data and weld examination results that inspector uses.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 requires covered process facilities to inspect and test equipment under recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, which is one reason plants keep a documented thickness history.

Georgia boiler and pressure vessel rules

In Georgia the Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, through its Engineering Division, inspects boilers and pressure vessels, and its rules sit in Chapter 120-3-26 of the state regulations. Equipment that falls under the program must be inspected regularly, subject to the exemptions the law lists, and accidents are reported to the office immediately by phone with a written report to follow. Thickness readings and weld examinations feed that regime by giving the owner and the commissioner's inspectors dependable data about the shell, heads and nozzles. We do not replace the state or the owner's authorized inspector; we supply measured, documented NDE results they can rely on.

Who does the work in Savannah

Atlantis has no office in Savannah. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, mill, shop or yard from outside the city for the agreed scope. They are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which is based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians set up, calibrate, perform and interpret the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews reports. The company's founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Procedures are written to your code, so the acceptance criteria are not invented on the day.

What the ultrasonic report contains

  • Component identification, location, material, nominal and minimum required thickness.
  • The procedure and revision used, the code and edition, and the acceptance criteria applied.
  • Instrument, probe, cable and calibration block identification, with calibration checks recorded.
  • Technician name and qualification level, and the examination date and surface temperature.
  • Thickness grids or point tables with the lowest reading flagged, or for welds, indication position, length, amplitude, depth and accept or reject.
  • Sketches or isometric markups so the next survey reads the same locations.

The format is built so an authorized inspector, an engineer or an auditor can follow the result back to a calibrated reading without a phone call.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Savannah

Savannah's climate and access conditions shape the schedule more than most buyers expect.

  • Salt air and humidity: outside surfaces rust quickly after wire brushing, so surface prep should be timed close to the reading, and dew on steel at dawn can affect couplant and cleanliness.
  • Summer heat: surfaces in direct sun get hot enough to affect probes and couplant, and work in shaded or cooler hours protects both people and data.
  • Terminal and port access: secure areas typically require a TWIC card and a site safety orientation, and crane or yard operations dictate when equipment can be taken out of service.
  • Mill outages: piping and vessel work clusters into shutdown windows, so thickness data has to be ready before the repair scope is frozen.
  • Tides and river traffic: work on dock structure and vessel plate follows the schedule of the berth.

Tell us the component list, access method and outage dates when you ask for a quote. We plan mobilization around those dates rather than promising a crew arrival time up front.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in Savannah

Match the method to the question. Use ultrasonic testing to size wall loss and to examine the inside of welds. Use magnetic particle testing to find surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel, for example the toes of crane welds. Use liquid penetrant testing for surface-breaking flaws on stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. Many jobs need two methods, because a thickness survey and a crack check answer different questions. For background on the method itself, read the UT service overview or the ultrasonic testing guide.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

If you would rather build a Savannah team than buy visits, Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training under SNT-TC-1A, with the UT practical simulator for hands-on repetition. Under that scheme your company certifies its own people through its written practice; see NDT training for Savannah employers and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker. An in-house Level II also reads your thickness data between our visits.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing measure in Savannah plants and terminals?
faq.a: It measures the remaining wall of steel by timing a sound echo through the metal. In Savannah that means piping at mills, tank shells, crane plate, hull and dock steel, so the owner can compare readings against minimum required thickness.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do UT inspection of welds as well as thickness?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians use angle-beam shear-wave probes calibrated on a reference block, scan the weld volume and heat-affected zone, and judge indications against the code named in your contract, such as AWS D1.1 or ASME Section V.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Savannah?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Savannah. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, mill, shop or yard for the agreed scope, and you receive a written report that traces every reading to a calibrated instrument.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be done on hot piping?
faq.a: Often yes. High-temperature probes and couplant are made for hot lines, and readings are corrected for metal temperature. The practical limit depends on the line temperature, access and the probe in use, so tell us the service conditions when you request a quote.

faq.q: Who is responsible for an API 510, 570 or 653 inspection when Atlantis does the UT?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and the fitness decision. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and thickness survey and gives that inspector complete, documented data to evaluate.

faq.q: What surface preparation does UT need on coated or rusted steel?
faq.a: The probe needs a clean contact patch, so loose scale, flaking paint and heavy rust are removed at each reading point. Thin, sound coating can sometimes be read through, but the procedure decides, and the owner approves any coating removal.

faq.q: Which Georgia agency regulates boilers and pressure vessels?
faq.a: The Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, through its Engineering Division, inspects boilers and pressure vessels in Georgia. Atlantis does not replace those inspections; we provide NDE data that the owner and inspectors can rely on.

faq.q: When should I choose magnetic particle testing instead of UT in Savannah?
faq.a: Choose magnetic particle testing when the question is a surface or near-surface crack in ferromagnetic steel, such as a crane weld toe. Choose UT when you need remaining wall or want to examine the inside of a weld.

faq.q: Can my own technicians learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis teaches UT Level 1 and Level 2 under ASNT SNT-TC-1A recommended practice. Your company then qualifies and certifies its technicians under its own written practice, and the course supports that employer-based process.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Savannah, GA | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Savannah, GA for crane welds, shipyard repairs, rigging, mill equipment and structural steel, mobilized to site. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Savannah, Georgia
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing) in Savannah, Georgia, searching for surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Typical jobs are welds on terminal cranes and yard equipment, rigging and lifting hardware, ship repair steel, mill machinery and fabricated structures. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. List the parts and welds through the MT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Savannah

A port that lifts millions of containers a year wears out hooks, pins and welds. Magnetic particle inspection is the quick, visual way to find the fatigue crack that grows from a weld toe or a sharp corner long before the part fails. Savannah's mix of terminals, mills, shipyard work and aerospace support gives the method plenty to do.

  • Cranes and container handling: welds on crane booms, portal legs and trolley frames, spreader twist-lock housings, lashing hardware, and the structure that carries the rails under rubber-tired gantries.
  • Rigging and lifting gear: hooks, shackles, padeyes, lifting lugs and spreader beams, which are often inspected before a heavy lift or after an overload event.
  • Ship repair and marine steel: repair welds on frames and brackets, doubler plates, deck fittings, mooring bitts and rudder or shaft supports on vessels that call for work at the river.
  • Paper and process plants: welds on carbon steel vessels and supports, lifting lugs on equipment, roll journals and housings, and structural steel around heavy machinery.
  • Fabrication and aerospace support: weldments, ground-support equipment, jacks, work stands and tooling for the aviation cluster, where a cracked fixture can damage far more than itself.

Almost all of this is ferromagnetic steel, which is exactly where magnetic particle inspection works well.

What magnetic particle inspection finds and what it misses

When a ferromagnetic part is magnetized, a crack that interrupts the field forces some of it to leak out of the surface. Fine iron particles applied to the part gather at that leakage and outline the crack. The method is quick, sensitive and light on equipment, but it has firm limits.

  • It finds: surface-breaking cracks, laps, seams and slightly subsurface discontinuities in ferromagnetic material such as carbon steel and low-alloy steel, including cracks too fine to see by eye.
  • It misses: anything in austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or titanium, because those metals do not carry a magnetic field; and deep flaws, which leak too little field to show at the surface.
  • It depends on direction: a crack shows best when it lies across the magnetic field, so each area is examined twice with the field turned about ninety degrees.
  • It depends on the surface: thick paint, scale and weld spatter weaken the indication and may need removal at the test area.

If the part is stainless or non-magnetic, liquid penetrant inspection in Savannah is the usual substitute, and if the question is remaining wall, ultrasonic thickness testing is the right tool.

How the technique is applied

Field work in Savannah is mostly done with a handheld electromagnetic yoke, which magnetizes the area between its legs. A yoke is portable, needs only a power point, and leaves no arc burns on the surface, so it suits crane steel, weld toes and lifting gear. Prods can be used on thick sections where a current has to be driven through the part, but they demand caution because they can burn the surface.

  • Visible dry or wet particles: colored powder or an aerosol suspension is applied over a contrast paint, which is practical outdoors on structures and welds.
  • Fluorescent particles: these glow under UV-A light in a darkened area, which gives higher sensitivity on critical welds and machined parts, and is typical of shop and tent-covered work.
  • Field strength check: a pie gauge or field indicator confirms that the magnetic field is adequate and correctly directed before particles go on.
  • Demagnetization: parts that will be welded, machined or placed in sensitive service are demagnetized afterward, because a residual field can pull particles and swarf onto surfaces.

Method rules come from ASTM E1444 and ASME Section V Article 7; read our summary of the Article 7 magnetic particle requirements or the magnetic particle testing guide for the detail.

What indications look like on Savannah steel

A crack indication is a sharp, tight, line of particles that follows the defect and is usually well defined against the background. A fatigue crack at a crane weld toe tends to run along the toe, while a hot crack in a repair weld may show across the weld bead or at a crater. Laps and seams in forged lifting hardware show as short lines at the surface, and a rounded smear of particles with a fuzzy edge often points to a subsurface source or a change in section rather than a crack.

Non-relevant indications are a daily reality. Sharp changes in geometry, the edges of welded attachments, magnetic writing left by earlier tests, and tool marks can all hold particles. The technician's job is to tell relevant indications from non-relevant ones, re-examine doubtful areas after light cleaning or demagnetizing, and report only what the procedure and code call for. Confusing the two either wastes repair effort or leaves a real crack in service, which is why Level II judgment and Level III oversight matter more than the equipment.

Weld inspection on crane structure is often repeated at intervals. Comparing today's photographs and sketches with the previous visit shows whether a stopped crack is truly stopped, and a record that is easy to read speeds that comparison.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Savannah work

  • ASME Section V Article 7: the examination method, including yoke lifting power, particle and light requirements, and the need for two examinations at roughly right angles.
  • ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6: magnetic particle methods and acceptance for pressure vessel welds.
  • ASME B31.3 and B31.1: piping examination requirements and acceptance tables for process and power piping.
  • AWS D1.1: structural steel, where magnetic particle examination is a recognized method for surface cracks in fillet and groove welds.
  • API 510, 570 and 653: in-service codes for vessels, piping and tanks. The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection; Atlantis performs the examination and reports each indication.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 expects covered facilities to inspect equipment under good engineering practice, and the state of Georgia, through the Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, regulates boilers and pressure vessels. Our job is to deliver crisp, code-referenced crack data to the people who own those decisions.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in Savannah. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, mill, shipyard or fabrication shop for the agreed scope. They work to a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician sets up the yoke, checks the field, applies the particles and interprets what is seen, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and the company holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification. If your contract names an acceptance code, the procedure is written to it, with the lifting-power check, the light levels and the demagnetization requirement stated in advance.

What the magnetic particle report contains

  • Component or weld identification, material, location, surface condition and test temperature.
  • Procedure number and revision, the code and edition, and the acceptance criteria used.
  • Equipment details: yoke or prod unit, calibration or lifting-power check, particle type and lot, UV-A intensity and ambient light readings where fluorescent particles are used.
  • Technician name and qualification level, date and weather conditions for outdoor work.
  • Each indication described by location, orientation, length and whether it is accepted or rejected, with a sketch or photograph where useful.
  • A note on demagnetization and post-test cleaning.

Rejected indications are reported to your representative as found, so repair and re-examination can be planned.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Savannah

  • Rain, dew and humidity: wet particle suspensions and paint contrast respond to moisture, and wind or rain on an open wharf can ruin a visible examination, so a tent or windbreak is often arranged.
  • Heat: steel in summer sun can exceed the temperature range the particle carrier or the procedure allows, and shaded or cooler working hours keep the method inside its limits.
  • Daylight versus darkness: fluorescent work needs a dark area, so a portable enclosure or night-time work may be needed outdoors.
  • Terminal access: secure port areas generally require a TWIC card and a safety orientation, and crane or lane operations decide when gear can be taken out of service.
  • Coatings: if crane steel is painted for corrosion protection, the owner decides how much coating may be removed at weld areas, and the procedure addresses coatings in advance.

Give us a part list, access method and out-of-service dates, and we plan mobilization to suit; we do not promise a crew arrival time without them.

Before any work starts, a short pre-job conversation settles the practical points: which welds are in scope, whether paint stays or goes, how power is supplied for the yoke, where a tent or dark enclosure can stand, and who signs off on rejected indications. Settling these on paper keeps a crane or yard from sitting idle while someone looks for a power point, and it keeps the report aligned with what the owner actually asked for.

Choosing between MT, PT and UT in Savannah

Use magnetic particle inspection for surface cracking on carbon and low-alloy steel, because it is fast and finds cracks that are tight and shallow. Use penetrant testing on stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals, or where particles cannot be applied. Use ultrasonic testing when the concern is wall loss or flaws inside a weld. The MT versus PT comparison sets out the trade-offs, and the national MT service page describes the method in general terms.

The Savannah mix of cranes, mills and marine steel rewards a repeatable record. Photographs of each weld before and after examination, clear sketches of indications and consistent location marks let a later technician confirm whether a repaired weld has stayed sound through another season of heavy lifts. Sending us the previous report with your request lets the examiner start from the same points rather than from scratch.

Training your own magnetic particle technicians

If you maintain cranes or heavy equipment in Savannah, a trained in-house technician can check critical welds more often than visits allow. Atlantis teaches MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 under SNT-TC-1A, and the magnetic particle training overview shows what is covered. Your company certifies its technicians under its own written practice, and we can help you draft it through written practice development. For local scheduling questions see NDT training for Savannah employers.

faq.q: What is magnetic particle inspection used for in Savannah?
faq.a: It finds surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. In Savannah that includes welds on terminal cranes, rigging and lifting gear, ship repair steel, mill machinery and fabricated structures.

faq.q: Will magnetic particle testing work on a stainless steel or aluminum part?
faq.a: No. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals do not carry the field the method needs. Liquid penetrant testing is normally used on those materials to find surface-breaking cracks instead.

faq.q: Do you need to remove paint before MT inspection?
faq.a: Thin, sound coating can sometimes stay if the procedure allows it, but thick paint, scale or spatter weakens indications. The owner decides how much coating is removed, and the procedure states the limit in advance.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Savannah office or lab for magnetic particle work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Savannah. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, mill, shipyard or shop, bring portable yokes and materials, and issue a written report for the agreed scope.

faq.q: Why is each area examined twice in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: A crack shows best when it crosses the magnetic field, so the field is applied in two directions about ninety degrees apart. That way cracks running in any direction are detected rather than only one orientation.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always needed after MT?
faq.a: Not always. It is required when a residual field could interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or service. The procedure and your specification state when demagnetization and residual field checks apply.

faq.q: Can fluorescent magnetic particle testing be done outdoors in Savannah?
faq.a: Yes, with a darkened area. A portable enclosure or night-time work provides the low ambient light and UV-A intensity the examination needs, so planning for light conditions belongs in the job scope.

faq.q: Who certifies the technicians who perform MT for Atlantis?
faq.a: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer qualifies and certifies its own personnel through a written practice. Atlantis technicians are qualified under that company practice, with an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my crew in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training aligned with SNT-TC-1A, and your company then certifies its technicians through its own written practice after the required training and experience.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Savannah, GA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Savannah, GA for stainless piping, welds, castings and non-magnetic parts at mills, terminals and shops. Request a quote today.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Savannah, Georgia
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, in Savannah, Georgia. The method reveals surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps on stainless steel, nickel alloys, aluminum, carbon steel and other non-porous materials. Typical work covers stainless process piping at paper and food plants, weld repairs, castings, marine fittings and fabricated parts. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. Describe the parts through the PT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Savannah

Penetrant testing earns its place wherever metal is not magnetic or where a crack has to be seen on a weld, casting or machined surface. Savannah has a lot of that kind of metal because its industries are wet, chemical, marine and food related, and these environments favor stainless steel and aluminum.

  • Paper and pulp plants: stainless pipe welds, heat exchanger shells, valve bodies, dryer and press-section components, and repair welds on process equipment that sees steam, moisture and cleaning chemicals.
  • Food and sugar processing: sanitary stainless pipe and tank welds, mixers, vessels and fittings where crack-like defects would trap product and shorten service life.
  • Marine and port equipment: aluminum and stainless fittings on vessels, bronze and nickel-aluminum propeller and valve components, hatch hardware and deck fittings exposed to salt water.
  • Aerospace support and machining: aluminum and stainless fabrications, ground equipment, tooling and machined parts around the airports, where a surface crack can end a component's life.
  • Fabrication shops: repair welds on carbon and alloy steel, root and cap passes on alloy piping, and castings and forgings received from suppliers.

If the metal is ordinary carbon steel and the concern is a crack, magnetic particle inspection in Savannah is often quicker; penetrant testing is the answer whenever magnetic methods do not apply.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean, dry surface and given time to be drawn into any opening by capillary action. After the excess is removed, a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out so the defect appears as a visible mark, in visible dye under white light or in fluorescent dye under UV-A light.

  • It finds: flaws that are open to the surface, such as fatigue cracks, shrinkage cracks, laps, cold shuts, porosity and incomplete fusion at the weld toe, on almost any non-porous metal, plastic or ceramic.
  • It misses: anything that does not break the surface, flaws filled with dirt, paint, oil or smeared metal, and defects on porous or very rough surfaces where the liquid bleeds out everywhere.
  • It depends on cleaning: grinding, blasting or machining can smear metal over a crack and close it, so etching or careful cleaning is often needed before the test.
  • It does not size depth: the indication shows length and position, not how deep the crack goes.

When a surface-breaking flaw has to be sized in depth, ultrasonic examination follows; see ultrasonic testing in Savannah.

How the technique is applied

The technique has a set sequence, and skipping steps is the most common reason indications are missed.

  1. Pre-clean the surface with solvent or detergent to remove oil, grease, paint and loose scale, then let it dry fully.
  2. Apply penetrant by spray, brush or dip; Type I fluorescent and Type II visible dye are both used, with the removal method chosen from water-washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent-removable materials.
  3. Allow the dwell time stated in the procedure, which depends on the material, the flaw type and the temperature.
  4. Remove the excess carefully without washing penetrant out of the defect.
  5. Apply developer in a thin, even layer, then inspect within the time window the procedure sets, and check again after the full development time.
  6. Post-clean the part so residue does not cause trouble in later welding or service.

Solvent-removable visible dye is the field workhorse because it is portable and needs no water supply. Detail on the requirements appears in the Article 6 liquid penetrant guide.

Indications and how they are judged

Penetrant indications are read against a defined background. A crack appears as a continuous or broken line, often with a crisp edge and a color that deepens as the developer dries. Porosity shows as scattered round dots, and a lap or cold shut as a short, slightly curved line. Because penetrant bleeds out and spreads, the technician watches the indication form during the development time and measures it at the point the procedure specifies, not at its largest later bleed-out.

False and non-relevant indications are common too. Rough weld ripples, machined threads, press fits and residue from poor cleaning can hold penetrant and imitate flaws. A good technician wipes the doubtful area, re-applies developer, and re-examines it, or re-cleans and repeats the full process. If an area was ground or blasted, the technician may require etching and re-testing before accepting a clean result, because a smeared surface can hide a real crack.

Acceptance depends on the code. Under most construction codes, linear indications are rejectable beyond a stated length, and rounded indications are evaluated by size and spacing. The report states which criterion was applied, so the repair decision rests on a named rule and not on opinion.

In hot, humid places such as Savannah, the same discipline is applied with extra attention to drying times and to the temperature of both the part and the materials. A clean result on a hot, wet surface proves very little, so the procedure is written to prevent that situation.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Savannah work

  • ASME Section V Article 6: the liquid penetrant examination method, including materials control, sensitivity, dwell and developer requirements.
  • ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8: penetrant methods and acceptance criteria for pressure vessel welds.
  • ASME B31.3 and B31.1: piping examination requirements and acceptance tables, with liquid penetrant named among the surface methods.
  • ASTM E165: the practice for liquid penetrant testing in general industry.
  • AWS D1.1 and D1.6: structural steel and stainless steel welding codes, where penetrant testing is a recognized surface examination for welds.
  • API 510 and 570: in-service codes for vessels and piping. The owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility; Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and reports every indication.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 sets expectations for mechanical integrity at covered facilities, and in Georgia the Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner inspects boilers and pressure vessels. Penetrant results are one input to those regimes, supplied as clear data for the people who decide.

Who carries out penetrant examinations

Atlantis has no office in Savannah. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, terminal or shop from outside the city for the agreed scope. What the penetrant report contains

  • Part or weld identification, material, surface condition and test temperature.
  • The procedure and revision, code and edition, and acceptance criteria used.
  • Penetrant, remover and developer type, manufacturer and batch numbers, and the penetrant removal method.
  • Dwell times, light conditions or UV-A intensity, and technician name and qualification level.
  • Each indication by location, type (linear or rounded), size and accept or reject decision, with sketch or photo.
  • A note on post-cleaning and any area that could not be examined.

Sketches and photographs make it simple for a repair crew to find the same spot, and for a later examiner to compare it.

Planning a penetrant job in Savannah

  • Temperature: the common standard range for the part and the materials is about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and Savannah summer steel in the sun can far exceed it, so work moves to shade or cooler hours or uses a qualified high-temperature procedure.
  • Humidity and dew: moisture left on a surface blocks penetrant entry, so cleaning and drying schedules matter more here than in dry climates.
  • Wind and rain: outdoor sprays drift and developer washes off, so temporary shelter is often part of the plan.
  • Cleanliness at food and paper plants: materials must be low in halogens and sulfur for stainless and nickel alloys, and residue must be removed so product contact is not affected.
  • Access and badging: port, mill and shipyard sites require orientation, and some require TWIC credentials for secure areas.

Tell us the material, surface condition and shutdown dates when you request a quote, and we plan mobilization around them without promising an arrival time in advance.

A short scoping call before the job saves time on site. It covers the alloy of each part, the finish, what cleaning agents the plant allows, whether fluorescent dye can be used under a darkened enclosure, and how rejected indications will be handled. For stainless and nickel alloys the owner's specification often limits the chlorine, fluorine and sulfur content of the materials, and confirming that first avoids rework and protects the equipment being tested.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT in Savannah

Choose liquid penetrant testing for surface-breaking cracks on stainless steel, aluminum, bronze and other non-magnetic metals, and for weld repairs where particles cannot be used. Choose magnetic particle testing for carbon and low-alloy steel when speed matters and the surface can be magnetized. Choose ultrasonic testing for wall thickness and internal weld flaws. The comparison of MT and PT explains the trade-offs, and the penetrant testing service overview covers the method more broadly.

For Savannah plants that repair stainless equipment during outages, a penetrant check after each weld repair catches the crack before the line is returned to service. Keeping the dye lot, the removal method and the dwell time in the record makes the next examination repeatable, and a clean photograph of each indication helps the repair crew find it quickly in a congested pipe rack or tank.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing find in Savannah industrial work?
faq.a: It finds cracks, laps, porosity and other flaws that are open to the surface. In Savannah it is used on stainless piping, weld repairs, castings, marine fittings and non-magnetic parts that magnetic particle testing cannot inspect.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing detect subsurface defects?
faq.a: No. Penetrant testing only reveals flaws that break the surface. A buried crack or lack of fusion inside a weld needs ultrasonic examination, which can see inside the section and estimate the position of the flaw.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much for dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: Grinding, blasting or paint can seal or smear over a crack so penetrant cannot enter. Careful cleaning, and sometimes etching, removes that cover, which is why many missed indications trace back to preparation.

faq.q: What temperature range is allowed for liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: The usual standard range for the part and penetrant materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, which matters for hot summer steel in direct sun.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be used on stainless steel at food or paper plants?
faq.a: Yes, using materials controlled for low halogen and sulfur content and cleaned off afterward. The procedure states these limits, and residue removal protects product contact surfaces and later welding.

faq.q: Should I choose penetrant or magnetic particle testing for a carbon steel weld?
faq.a: Magnetic particle inspection is often faster on carbon steel, but penetrant is a valid choice when particles are not practical, the surface cannot be magnetized or the code calls for it. Your specification decides.

faq.q: Who is responsible for the inspection when Atlantis does PT under API 510 or 570?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility for the inspection and the repair decision. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and supplies documented indications for that inspector to evaluate.
